blocks.text: The chapter carefully names Pihahiroth, Migdol, Baal-zephon, and the sea as Israel’s camping place. Those names preserve the narrative’s route and setting, but identifying each site on a modern map—and therefore locating the crossing precisely—remains disputed. The passage itself supplies the sequence of places without settling every modern reconstruction.

Keeping the chapter’s own place names in view prevents a familiar modern map from being treated as the only possible route. The geographical uncertainty does not erase the text’s setting; it distinguishes the named route in the narrative from later attempts to match every location with a modern site.

Exodus 14 is a climactic deliverance scene, but the book does not end with escape from Egypt. Exodus moves from oppression and deliverance to covenant, covenant breach and renewal, the construction of the tabernacle, and the arrival of divine glory. Reading these movements together keeps the sea crossing within the book’s larger account rather than treating departure from Egypt as its endpoint.
